text:
<margin>Commentary by Su</margin> Not knowing but striving for learning, hearing and seeing more each day, yet having no way to unify it, one cannot avoid being burdened. Confucius said, "Hear much, choose what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day one comes to know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss>, looking back, all acts of pretense are false. To remove falsehood and restore one's nature is called "diminishing." Confucius asked Zigong, "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with a single thread." When the mind is forgotten and becomes pure, and the nature is restored, this is called diminishing. If the false is not yet fully removed, even to the point of forgetting the act of forgetting, the mind cannot be pure and restore the nature without remainder. Only then can one act without losing the state of non-action. People all have the desire to seize the world and the reasoning behind things, so they initiate affairs and seek to control them. When the heart is revealed externally, things will dislike it, which makes success impossible. The sage performs non-action, so he has no affairs. When his heart is revealed externally, things find peace. Although he does not seek to control the world or its reasoning, because he acts this way, the world and its reasoning become harmonious and peaceful.

<margin>Commentary by Lü</margin> Engaging in learning means one has not yet heard the <term>Tao</term>. Not having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must be broad in seeking it, therefore it is said, "increase." Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> means one has already heard the <term>Tao</term>. Having heard the <term>Tao</term>, one must inevitably practice non-action, therefore it is said, "diminish." Diminishing and further diminishing still does not escape from having intentional action. One must also diminish the act of diminishing itself, and only then reach the state of non-action. Non-action means there is no intentional action, which is called being silent and unmoved. "Doing nothing, yet leaving nothing undone" refers to the state where, upon being stimulated, one perfectly comprehends all the affairs of the world. To act through non-action to reach the ultimate non-action is what is meant by the constant. Learning that is free from worry is called spirit. The method of the spirit is the <term>Tao</term>. Who but the most divine can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, one knows that to take the world, one must always use non-action; if one uses intentional action, it is not enough to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary by Huang Maocai</margin> Only after one knows everything can one speak of learning, so learning aims to increase day by day. Only after one can do anything can one speak of the <term>Tao</term>, so the <term>Tao</term> aims to diminish day by day. Yet, "increasing" is something one can pursue, while "diminishing" is perhaps difficult to force. Only those with the utmost clarity can instantly cast off their burdens and arrive at the state of non-action. Thus, they can act in such a way that nothing is left undone, and their applications are inexhaustible, governing the world with ease.

<margin>Commentary by Xizhai</margin> Engaging in learning is for the sake of seeking knowledge, thus it increases day by day. Engaging in the <term>Tao</term> is for the sake of removing falsehood, thus it diminishes day by day. If knowledge does not reach the limit, the diminishing will be incomplete; thus, the "increasing" is the foundation for the "diminishing." If one diminishes and diminishes again until falsehood is gone and the truth is complete, then one arrives at non-action. When one reaches non-action, there is nothing one does that is not non-action. This is not easily discussed in terms of increase or decrease. When it comes to the height of non-action, even though the world is vast, it is unified by a single thread. If one creates affairs through intentional action, it is hard to find a moment of peace. If even one thing creates entanglement and contradiction, how much more so with the complexity of the whole world?

The sage has no constant mind. He makes the hearts of the common people his own heart. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good, for the <term>De</term> <gloss>Virtue/Power</gloss> of goodness is attained. To those who are trustworthy, I am trustworthy; to those who are not trustworthy, I am also trustworthy, for the <term>De</term> of trust is attained. In the world, the sage is cautious and keeps his heart simple and unadorned. The common people all focus their ears and eyes upon him, and the sage...

<summary>This page contains classical commentaries on the early chapters of the Tao Te Ching, discussing the paradox of learning (which increases) versus practicing the Tao (which diminishes). It emphasizes the transformation from intentional action to the spontaneous effectiveness of the sage.</summary>
<keywords>Tao, De, Non-action, Sage, Learning, Diminishing, Increasing, Su, Lü, Huang Maocai, Xizhai</keywords>
